newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary says NATO should take in Romania, Slovenia.
newsitem.headline: Hungary says NATO should take in Romania, Slovenia.

text.p: Hungary on Monday made a last-minute appeal to NATO's Madrid summit to include Romania and Slovenia in the first wave of enlargement, saying the move would ensure stability in south-eastern Europe.

"I think a longer list could contribute to the stability and security in the region and the accession of these two countries would certainly contribute to bilateral relations," Hungarian Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs told Reuters prior to his departure for Madrid.

U.S. President Bill Clinton has named Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic as the three members he favours for the first group of new entrants and has said he will resist other NATO states' attempts at the summit, starting Tuesday, to broaden the first wave to include Romania and Slovenia.
Kovacs said Hungary's geographical position bordering fellow NATO aspirants Slovakia, Romania and Slovenia, gave it special reasons for supporting a larger eastward enlargement.

"It is our genuine interest that we want to maintain good neighbourly relations with our neighbours including Romania and Slovenia that now are struggling very much to get into the first wave of enlargement," he said.

In recent years Hungary has considerably improved ties with all its adjacent states by concluding friendship treaties on borders and the protection of national minorities which had eluded previous post-communist governments.

Kovacs said that however many states made up the first group, a second wave of entrants should also be named with a possible time frame in order to limit the perception of a new division in Europe between new members and others left waiting.
"(Naming a second wave) is important because Hungary and all present-day and new members of NATO would like to prevent any kind of new division as a side effect of the enlargement," he said.
"That could be avoided by naming countries in the second wave and giving an approximate date," he said.

Kovacs said a summit meeting between the prime ministers of Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland to be held on August 22 in the Polish city of Krakow would be an opportunity for the three countries to coordinate their approaches to accession talks expected to begin in September.
But he ruled out any joint sessions during the three countries' negotiations.
"We will exchange views on how to harmonise our position, but of course Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic will not negotiate with NATO as a homogeneous group."
Kovacs said he expected to put Hungary's NATO membership to a national referendum in the autumn during the accession talks.

"I could imagine an autumn referendum provided that by then we know the major conditions," he said, adding that there would be no question of holding the referendum at the same time as Hungarian parliamentary elections due next spring.
"Next year's election would be too late and the election and the referendum could not be organised in parallel," he said.
He described the imminent invitation to join NATO as a "breakthrough in Hungary's Euro-Atlantic integration", including its efforts to join the European Union.
"The invitation to join NATO is proof that Hungary has met the general political and economic criteria also to join the EU," he said.
